I do not intend to make any comments at the moment; I simply wish to ask, I think, three questions of the minister. The first is this: As respects his figure of operating ratio for last year, which he gave as 129 and a fraction, I draw his attention to the fact that it was given in last ' ear's statement as 124 and a fraction. As long as he is certain that his figure is not an error, I am quite prepared to take his statement that it is a correction of last year's figure.
I shall be glad to verify the statement. I gave it in good faith, and assumed it was correct.

I ask the question particularly for this reason : The 'loss last year was given in the same statement as $69,000,000, whereas the minister to-day corrects it and reduces the loss for 1920 to $67,000,000. Consequently, I would think, were he altering the operating ratio, he would alter it by diminishing it; instead of that, it is a very substantial increase.
The next question is this: In referring to the construction programme for this year, the minister stated that nothing would be done save in cases where construction had already proceeded to the point where the track was laid. I would like the minister to explain just what that means: how much of the track; the ballasting, or merely the construction of the grade; or does it include, indeed, the laying of the rails?
It includes the rails.
Then I would understand that there were no new rails to be laid-not a mile of rails to be laid?
That is correct.

The next question is this: In stating the invested capital in the railways that will subsequently be included in the entire unified svstem, he fixed the figure at one-and-a-half billions as subscribed by the public. I would understand by that, he means the public of this and other countries, not simply of this Dominion?
Exactly.

The last question is this: The minister referred to an investigation that was to be conducted for some purpose not any too closely defined, but he gave no intimation as to what would be

the character of the commission or committee or individual who is to investigate. Is it under the Inquiries Act, is it to be a committee of this House a royal commission, or what?

My hon.
friend refers to the investigation of the board?

I really hardly know how to describe it because the minister did not describe it himself. He said there was to be an investigation concurrently with the co-ordination. What it is to investigate I do not know very well-finances, I think, or something like that. Is the investigation to be by a committee of this House, or a commission, or is to be under the Inquiries Act?
That will be a matter for the new board. If it is thought advisable to have an investigation likewise by a committee of the House constituted for that purpose, very well.
What the minister had in mind, though, was an investigation under the new board after its appointment?

Yes. I
might point out to my right hon. friend that there has been considerable criticism in the press of recent statements issued by the National Railways; they have been analyzed in detail in the press, and the criticism has been made that the statements put out by the railways were incorrect. One of the first things the new board will do will be to verify the figures that have already been given out. The thought I had in mind was that the statements that are given out should be of such a character that the people of this country will rely upon them.
Meaning it will be done by or under the board?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, when hon. gentlemen who sit opposite occupied seats on this side of the House, it was customary to delay discussion of the annual report of the Minister of Railways until after it had been printed and distributed and the members had had an opportunity to study the figures contained in the report. I have no intention this afternoon-and I fancy that those who sit in this part of the House will for the most part delay discussion of this report-of following the Minister of Rail-

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
ways through the comprehensive report that he has presented to the House. He has given to us sufficient statistics to justify study by the members, and we will at some time before his Main Estimates are considered make opportunity to discuss such features of his statement today as in the opinion of members in this part of the House should be reviewed.
I would, however, like to say just a few words in passing with reference to certain features of the railway situation, and particularly with reference to the carrying out of the promise of co-ordination as contained in the Speech from the Throne. It is now some five weeks since co-ordination first broke upon the House, and during that time an anxious House and an interested public have looked for a realization of co-ordination by action of the Government. The statement made by the Minister of Railways to-day would appear to work out co-ordination by promising the bringing into force of the Canadian National Railway Act of 1919 at an indefinite time, and the appointment of a committee of the House to consider the question of railway rates. As I understood the minister's statement, those were the two declarations of policy which he made to us this afternoon.
It is very difficult for us on this side of the House to appreciate the necessity for the delay. The minister has stated to us that the matters involved in the appointment of a unified board are so important and so difficult that it is impossible for the Government at this time to appoint its board and to carry on the policy of unification that was contemplated when the Canadian National Railway Act of 1919 was passed. Those who were interested in the campaign last fall and followed the speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite will be surprised, I am sure, that they do not feel they have yet a sufficient knowledge of the railway situation to carry out even the appointment of a unified board. The policy of the late government was a clean-cut policy so far as the administration of our railways is concerned. In 1917, when the Canadian Northern system was taken over, the Government of Canada assumed a tremendous responsibility, assumed it at a time when in the opinion of the Canadian people and of Parliament there was no policy open to the government except to do as the government did, and when any other policy would have broken down at the most critical time in the history
of Canada the whole transportation system of this Dominion. The difficulty with the Canadian Northern arose at a time when the transportation facilities of Canada were groaning under war traffic, and had the road been permitted to go into liquidation there is no question that it would have not only destroyed the usefulness of the Canadian Northern system itself, but it would also have paralysed the whole transportation system of Canada.
I am not going to discuss whether the arrangement of 1917 was a wise one or not. The fact is that it is the one that was adopted by the Parliament of Canada. The government was face to face with the problem of providing for the management of the railways which were taken over by the Canadian Government at that time. Two plans for the management of its railway property were open to the government of the day. One was to manage the railways under a department of government, to continue the whole, railway system of Canada under the political management under which the Intercolonial had been managed and controlled for forty years prior to that time; the other was to provide for independent control in the management. The policy adopted by the late government was to try out, perhaps for the first time in the history of railway economics, government ownership with independent control in management. The policy adopted at that time provided for the complete removal of the management of the nationally owned railways from political control. That condition prevailed down to 1919 when the arrangements for taking over the Grand Trunk were completed, and in order to continue the policy that had been adopted in 1917 the Canadian National Railway Act of 1919 was passed. That act provided for a new board which would take over the combined systems. It provided for the taking over of both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk systems, so that we would have a unified management, under which we could get co-ordination. And perhaps those who have studied the Canadian railway situation will agree that there must be a ruthless co-ordination of these systems if we are to see daylight through our railway problem.
Now, under the original arrangement with the Grand Trunk the Grand Trunk officials were continued in office. They were continued in office for the reason that it was felt that in order to enable them to pre-



C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
perly prepare and conduct their case before the arbitration tribunal they should have access to the books and records of the company and should be in complete touch not only with the records but with the operation of the system. But after there had been default in the completion of the arbitration proceedings at the time specified-a default which in the opinion of the government of the day was a deliberate default on the part of the officials of the Grand Trunk, a deliberate attempt to postpone the arbitration proceedings-and after the government had refused to extend the period for the completion of the arbitration, it was agreed between the Government of Canada and the Grand Trunk itself that the government should be given immediate control of the Board of Management of the system, and this was carried out, and a new board was appointed. The question might further be asked why the government did not at the time provide for the unified management, why at the time it did not provide for a central control? That occurred in the early months of 1921.
In May.

And a board was appointed at that time, an independent board, the board as it exists to-day. On that board the Government appointed executive officers of the Grand Trunk, and they appointed as chairman Sir Joseph Fla-velle. The Deputy Minister of Justice was a member of the board, and Mr. Dupuis. The reason why an independent board was appointed was in order that it might be given an opportunity to investigate such details as might be necessary to carry out the amalgamation in management of two great railway systems. It was thought at that time that it would result in a more efficient means for the appointment of a central board and for its control in management if an independent board for the Grand Trunk railway were given an opportunity to study the details of the Grand Trunk system and its requirements, and that then the two boards would be utilized for one purpose of working out a central control. As early as October of last year we had, in the opinion of the government, reached the time when it would have been possible to carry out the provisions of the Canadian National Railway Act of 1919. We had reached the time when the two boards could have been dispensed with and a central board appointed. The question

may fairly be asked why the government did not carry out that policy? The answer consists in the fact that we were in the midst of a federal election, and it was felt that it would have been unwise for the government to have possibly complicated the situation by the appointment of a board pending the result of the poll. Hon. gentlemen opposite will no doubt commend us on our foresight in that connection. The fact is that the new board was not appointed, but early as the month of October the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, in making a statement in the maritime provinces as to his view of how the eastern lines of the government owned railways should be managed, made practically the statement that was made by the Minister of Railways to-day. He stated in the maritime provinces in the early days of the month of October that in his opinion there should be a grand division-a grand division that would manage not only the Intercolonial and National Transcontinental but such of the Grand Trunk lines as might be brought within its jurisdiction. So that as early as the month of October last it was the opinion of the late government that the time had arrived when the provisions of the Act of 1919 might be brought into force.
We commend the Minister of Railways for his policy in reference to the Intercolonial. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) put up a very strong argument the other day in support of the return of the Intercolonial to political control. He gave us a very interesting historical account of the conditions under which the maritime provinces entered confederation, and urged that section 145 of the British North America Act made it compulsory for this Government to continue the management of the Intercolonial railway under the system that had obtained from 1878 down to the time it was placed under the management of the Canadian National Railway Board. He at the same time made a further statement with reference to rates-stated it as his opinion that the question of rates upon the Intercolonial was one which should not be determined by commercial considerations at all but should be regulated and controlled by the requirements of trade. I am not so sure that the position taken by the hon. gentleman as to rates can be disputed. I am not so sure that it is not possibly fundamental in the pact of Confederation that there should be interprovincial trade, and inter-

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
provincial trade-it matters not whether it originates in the East or in the West, or whether it originates centrally for the East or for the West-must be on conditions that will permit that trade to be carried on. So I submit that possibly the position taken by the member for Cumberland in reference to rates is one that will commend itself to the House. But what I am glad to note by the statement delivered by the Minister of Railways this afternoon is, that the Intercolonial is to be permitted to function as a part of the great national railway system, and I am sure the fact that the Intercolonial should be treated in this way will commend itself to the House. Unquestionably it will best serve the people whom it was built to serve, and whom it was intended to serve, as a part of the national system rather than by reverting to a position of " splendid isolation."
I am not going to attempt to deal with the financial portion of the statement of the minister except to say this: That the improvement in round figures of $20,000,000 in operating revenue between 1920 and 1921 is a record which brings comfort to those who were chiefly responsible for the system that was adopted in respect of the national railway properties. As I understand it, and as I understood the figures of the minister, on the whole of the government properties, including the Grand Trunk, the operating improvement was $20,000,000 in round figures. The real test of a railway's strength, and the real test of administrative skill, does not occur in periods of prosperity and buoyancy of traffic, it occurs in periods of adversity and depression. And the fact that during a year such as 1921 we were able to show, in connection with the government railways, a result as satisfactory as that reported to the House to-day is very creditable indeed. It is unquestionably a good showing, and that statement will scarcely be disputed. I would like to ask hon. gentlemen who questioned the policy of the late government with reference to the property which came over to the Canadian people if there is amongst them those who still feel that the result for 1921 would have been better had we had private ownership and private control.
I wish to refer in a general way to the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite with reference to the railway policy in Canada, not so much now as during the later months of last year. It was a popular political pastime for the opponents of the
58i
late government to lay at the feet of that government the blame for all our railway troubles. I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) when he says it matters little which political party was to blame, or whether both were entitled to censure for the conditions that led up to the situation in which we found ourselves in 1917 and again in 1919, and I entirely agree with him when he says that the people of Canada must bear their fair share of the blame. I am sure, as far as the Liberal-Conservative party was concerned, that in 1904, and again in 1908, we did everything we could to convince the Canadian people that the construction of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific was a mistake. There is no question about our position in that regard. The people decided otherwise in terms that could by no possible means be misunderstood, and for that reason there is no question that they are entitled to some share of the blame, if blame attaches, for the position in which we found ourselves later.
In the confession of political faith of the Liberal faith, and the confession of political faith of hon. gentlemen opposite, contained in the Ottawa platform of 1919, and in the public press, particularly in the press of the latter months of last year, and on the public platform of the same period and since this House opened, hon. gentlemen have charged the late government and the Liberal-Conservative party with the deliberate intention of destroying the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental by encouraging construction of the Canadian Northern system, and charging that the Canadian Northern system was deliberately built into territory which should have been the territory of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Hon. gentlemen who take that position might, with profit, refer to the views held by the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. His views are very clearly set forth in the discussion in 1914 on the question of the advance which was then under consideration to the Canadian Northern railways. It will be found in Hansard 13th May, 1914. In his discussion of the resolution introduced by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden providing for a loan to the Canadian Northern in that year, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid said in part:
I may confess at once that I have long believed that this country requires three transcontinental railways and although this theory has been sometimes controverted, in this House and out of it, I have never seen any reason to

C. N. B.-Minister's Statement
change my opinion
For my part I can say that I have always favoured the efforts of our two fellow citizens,-
Mackenzie and Mann.
-whose names have been mentioned several times by my right hon. friend, and who have applied themselves for many years to the task of binding the continent with another band of steel. The late Government were not slow to interest themselves in the enterprise and to favour it as much as they could.

Irt 1899, or thereabouts, after we came into office, we asked Parliament to give them assistance to extend the railway system then in existence in Manitoba eastward to the end of Lake Superior. If I remember rightly, we gave them a cash subsidy of $6,400 a mile for that length of railway. Later, in 1903, we induced Parliament to give them a guarantee of $13,000 a mile for a line of railway running through Manitoba to the city of Edmonton. Afterwards, in 1908, we asked Parliament to give them another guarantee of bonds to provide for several branch lines which would be feeders of the line in the Prairie Provinces. In 1911, as has been explained by my right hon. friend, it was considered that the system would not be complete unless it were extended eastward to the St. Lawrence and eventually to the Maritime Provinces, that is to say, unless it were made a transcontinental railway, and in that year we asked Parliament to give to the enterprise from Port Arthur to Montreal a guarantee of bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile.

We are told that these companies are to be united in a transcontinental system, and with that object I agree.
My right hon. friend said, and I altogether agree with him, that we cannot allow this enterprise to fail. We have too much money in it not only the money of the country, but of the Provinces and of the bond holders themselves. It is therefore, necessary that we should assist this enterprise.
My right hon. friend says that we are to go into partnership with Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann and the Canadian Northern railway. These are the very words of the Prime Minister. That being so, is it unreasonable to ask that in that partnership we should be the leading and not the junior partner? * [DOT] *
I said a moment ago, and I repeat, that this enterprise must go on. It has been conceived for the benefit of the Canadian people. We require this Railway. My right hon. friend said he would not let it go into liquidation. It must not go into liquidation, but we should have the con-tol of it.
<Since we must go into partnership with the Canadian Northern railway let us see that we are the master, and not the servant.
We have helped them in the past, I for my part, have been an admirer of their energy and enterprise.
That was the policy advocated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1914. In 1917, when the financial difficulties of the Canadian Northern forced them to come to the Canadian parliament, the policy of the late government was in direct line with that advocated by the right hon. leader of the Liberal party in 1914. I submit to the House that when hon. gentlemen opposite attempt to disassociate themselves from the construction of the Canadian Northern and all that 
led up to its completion, they cannot, in the records of parliament, find anything to support that position. The hon. Prime Minister, the other day, urged that it was under the late government that more than 4,000 miles of the Canadian Northern came into operation. That I am willing to concede. The point I want to make is this, that practically all the main line construction of the Canadian Northern was effected under charters issued by the Liberal government prior to 1911, and the subsidies, with the exception of the subsidy covering the railway from Prince Albert to the British Columbia boundary, were largely, if not exclusively authorized by the former Liberal government.
I stated before and I repeat now that I do not propose to discuss the report further, but I shall have an opportunity of doing so when the general estimates of the Railway Department are considered.

This old and familiar subject of railways is rather tempting to one who has been in this House as long as myself. Let me at once congratulate the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) upon the very able and excellent presentation which he has made of the case to the committee. I am sure that there is no misunderstanding the real situation as presented by the minister and that, as he continues in the administration of the railway affairs of this country, the people generally and this House will be satisfied that no mistake has been made in putting the hon. gentleman at the head of this very important department.
The history of railways in Canada is rather an old one, and nothing comes closer to the interest of the (people generally than the operation of our railways. Perhaps, this is not the time to go at any length into this question, and if any person of less incisive speech than the hon. member for Lanark (Mr, Stewart) had replied to the Minister of Railways, I am not sure that I would have said anything at all on this subject. Although always opposed to the hon. gentleman politically, I have great admiration for his talent and ability; he has a great knack of making things appear just exactly what they are not. After my hon. friends across the way came into power, there became noticeable amongst them an absolute neglect or forgetfulness of time; they apparently became possessed of one divine attribute in that one day

C. N. B.-Minister's Statement
was to them as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day.
The hon. member for Lanark reminded the committee that, in 1919, they passed an act for the purpose of amalgamating the railways. Well, 1919 is a good while ago. I was in the House at that time and I think the hon. member for Lanark was also. If I remember correctly, the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) who now leads the Opposition, had charge of that bill. If he had not charge of it, he was very industrious, as he always is, in the promotion of it. The bill was introduced in such a hurry that, after it had received its second reading, eleven clauses were added to it.

What bill does the
hon. member refer to?

The bill for the
amalgamation of the railways, chapter 13 of the acts of the first session of 1919. I think my right hon. friend had charge of it. The year 1919 has passed; so have 1920 and 1921, and now we are barely started with 1922. And although lately hon. gentlemen opposite have had no control over these matters, during those years, although there was such feverish haste over introducing the bill that it had to be put before the House and put into committee before it was all properly drafted, nothing was done towards bringing about this amalgamation. To-day, however, I find the hon. member for Lanark metaphorically shaking his fist in the face of the minister and saying:	" Here you have
been in power since the 27th of December last, and nothing has been done in connection with the matter." Is it not a little marvellous what a difference it makes whose ox is being gored?
I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite are highly critical that we are taking so much time in carrying out other matters of this kind, when during ten long years with opportunities which we do not possess even now, they did nothing at all. Will the hon. member for Lanark take these matters into serious consideration and put himself for a moment in the other fellow's place? He himself has been a Minister of Railways, if not for a longer time, at all events, for about as long a time as the present minister, and I find no monuments standing to his memory.

Perhaps the hon. member would agree that the statement just
read by the minister is some monument itself to what was done by the late government.

All I can say is that for ten years we were hearing statements from ministers of my right hon. friend's party, and in them we found nothing at all of the hopeful note that is contained in the statement made to-day.
It is a monument to what had been done before the present minister came into office.

As regards the will of the people, and monuments, I say to my right hon. friend that, in 1904, the railway policy of the Liberal party was submitted to the people of Canada, and it received almost unanimous approval from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The great leader of the Liberal party of
5 p.m. those days did not expend one dollar in carrying forward the railway policy of that party until he first made it the main issue in the election of 1904, and having received the mandate of the people of Canada to go on with this work, he went on with it. Therefore, it must be admitted that the policy of the Liberal party was fully and squarely presented to the jury of the electorate of Canada, and that the work was proceeded with only after the electorate had given full consent to the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier to go on with the work. What happened? The government that has just gone out of office and its predecessor in office, the Borden administration, came into charge of this policy before it was completed and brought to its full fruition; they had charge of the business of completing the construction of the railway and managing it for ten years, and the same people who said to Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government "Build the railway," said to that administration after ten years of management: "You must be kicked out; you are not fit to be relied on."

What did Sir
Wilfrid Laurier and his government inform the people this railway would cost them?

Neither Sir Wilfrid
and his government, nor any other government could say how much would be the cost of an enterprise comprising as many miles as this. There has been a great deal of misrepresentation about some statement alleged to have been made by the

Minister of Finance of that day. It has been answered and cleared up a hundred times; but hon. gentlemen opposite, wishing to make political capital out of that statement and to put the Liberal party in wrong in connection with it, persist, notwithstanding those various and multitudinous statements, in still standing by the old statement. Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself, as far as I know, never made any definite statement as to what the road was going to cost.

Will my hon. friend explain now why the statement that the road was going to cost $13,000,000 was made? He says that one hundred and one reasons have been given. What was the reason for that statement?
We were told in an estimate issued by the late government, of which my hon. friend was an ornament, that this magnificent building was going to cost $5,000,000. What is it going to cost now?
I could not tell you.
Perhaps $15,000,000 before we are through with it. Will my hon. friend explain that difficulty and that difference?	*

My hon. friend is quite profuse with his language, and somewhat regardless of his figures sometimes, and I am sure he will give an explanation, whether satisfactory or not. When a certain man of old was asked who gave him his sight, he answered: " I know not; but one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." I was expecting, Mr. Chairman, that I would be given right of way this afternoon after having kept so very quiet since the beginning of the session; but I observe there is no consideration to be gained from some hon. members by being quiet. My point is that the Canadian people gave their assent to the railway policy of the Laurier government; that it was necessary for the full development of the country to carry that policy into effect; that when the party to which I belong left office in 1911, we passed over the National railway property in its then condition to the incoming administration; and that their financial critic when making his
budget speech in February, 1912, stated that that property was a splendid asset to the country. What he stated then has been often quoted in the House since, and it has never been contradicted because it cannot be.
Now then, the general railway policy of the Laurier administration was endorsed by the people, and we carried the Transcontinental almost to completion. And when we handed it over to the incoming administration, and one of their leading financial men said, "It is all right, it is money well expended, it is a splendid national asset," our responsibility ended. If the new' administration spoiled the road in the building; if they broke the contracts and interfered with the arrangements we had with other companies in regard to it; if they made it impossible to carry out the original arrangement of which the people of Canada approved; if they made a wreck of the whole thing-and it was a wreck when handed over to us the other day-who is responsible? After the Government has been in power for a few weeks, hon. gentlemen, like the priest with the Levite, pass by on the other side; they say they had nothing at all to do with this wreckage. Is that fair? Will the hon. member for Parry Sound go home and pray over that, and then say that his attitude is right? Surely it is not an attitude which should be taken by fair minded men to-day. If the road has not been a success during ten years of administration by hon. gentlemen opposite, that is no fault of ours. If they spoiled the grade in the building of the remainder of the Transcontinental road and brought about a condition under which the contracts with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk could not be carried out, that is no fault of ours. But the condition faces us, and we must make the most of it. We have promised to give government ownership a square deal and a fair trial, and that we are bound to do; we are bound to give the people an opportunity to see how this thing works out.
I do not wish anybody to have any misapprehensions about my own position in the matter. I happen to be a member of this Government, and I stand by the position the Government has taken in regard to giving this road a square deal and making the most of it. The records of this House will show that ever since there was talk of the Government taking these roads over, as a matter of conscientious belief I was op-
920	COMMONS
C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
posed to that being done. I was not in favour of government ownership, because I have always believed that you cannot get the same results from government ownership and government management that you get under private ownership and private enterprise. But I am anxious and willing that everything shall be done in order to make this road a success, and I hope it will be a success. In that respect the statement made by the minister to-day is encouraging; it shows some signs of an advance in the right direction.
There is one other thing I wish to say about this railway situation. I cannot understand how hon. gentlemen sitting in opposition can talk as they do about Portland and the branch lines of the Grand Trunk in the United States, having regard to the attituude they themselves have taken. Since Parliament opened, several criticisms have been made about the attitude of the present Government with regard to the situation at Portland. We did what we could to prevent the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, particularly that portion of it which is in the United States. We took the ground that hundreds and millions of dollars had been spent in this country to establish railways running from east to west; that millions had been spent in the deepening of the St. Lawrence and the enlarging of canals to make navigation possible, so that we would be an independent nation and capable of carrying on our own affairs. But after all that money had been expended, the Meighen administration went down to Portland and established there, in a foreign country, what is practically a national port of this country. Can anybody stand by a policy of that kind? They bought not only 2,000 miles of road in a foreign country, but they virtually bought a port which must be maintained. Will anybody for one moment say to the Canadian people: "We were advised by the late government to spend millions in buying this road and establishing this terminus in a foreign country, and now we are to .starve it by cutting off every avenue of traffic leading to it "? If hon. gentlemen opposite are consistent, they must be in favour of diverting traffic toward that port, thereby starving such places as Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, Sydney, and St. John.
Cape Breton.

Cape Breton is so well off and so wealthy that they could not starve

it; if they could, they would have done it long ago. I may tell my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Stewart) that I have before me a record of the various resolutions that were proposed while the discussion on the Grand Trunk railway acquisition was proceeding in the House. Resolution after resolution was moved by hon. gentlemen then in opposition, now on the right of the Speaker, asking that delay should take place; that there should be investigation; that the bill should not be read until further information had been obtained. I find on looking at the division lists the illustrious name of my hon. friend from Lanark, indicating, by his vote, his desire to rush pell-mell to Portland and establish there, in a foreign country, the national ierminus of all our railway systems. My good friend from St. John City (Mr. Baxter), who accepted office in the late administration, knowing the history of matters in connection with Portland, knowing that a stage had been reached which made a retracing of steps impossible, now finds fault, because forsooth, we are not cutting off Portland and cutting off all our connections with the United States. It is far from businesslike, far from courageous on the part of my hon. friends to whine about Portland and our connection with the United States when that is a condition which they themselves brought about. Our national status requires that we should have our own ports on the Pacific and on the Atlantic, independent of any foreign country.
I condemn, as I have always done, the idea of linking up our railways with the railway systems of the United States and with United States ports, as was done by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition and his predecessor as Prime Minister of this country. Those who are old members of the House recall the battles that were fought over this question. They know, and we know in the maritime provinces, particularly in Nova Scotia, that one of our grievances against the outgoing government was their taking over coal [DOT]mines in the United States, the output of which must necessarily compete with ours, thus destroying a part of the market for our coal. It was a near-sighted policy on the part of my right hon. friend and those who sat in council with him, to buy coal mines in the United States capable of producing something like two or three million tons of coal annually and to admit that coal into the markets of this country free of duty. While that coal output was controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company,

C. N. It.-Minister's Statement
duty had to be paid upon it when it came into Canada, and that was a matter of business; we could say nothing about it. But we bought the Grand Trunk, with its \arious railway lines, its coal mines, and everything belonging to it, and if the coal now pays duty on coming into Canada, it is simply a case, so far as the Government is concerned, of taking money out of one pocket and putting it into the other.
Was the hon. gentleman opposed to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway, and is he still?

Always was, am
to-day, and shall continue to be. My hon. friend knows, and my record in this House will show, that I was always opposed to any property being acquired to be run by the Government, particularly the government of that day. I feel rather humiliated that I have never been able to impress upon my hon. friend where I stood on this matter. However, there is hope yet.

My hon. friend quotes
scripture of.tener than he does politics.

Of some people it
can be said as was said of Ephraim, "Ephraim is joined to idols; let him alone." I have always been opposed to this policy of buying railways in the United States because, as every member of this House knows, we have no control, so far as legislation goes, over these properties in a foreign country. We cannot pass one line of legislation regarding them. They come under the legislation of the different states through which they run, and we have no representation in those state legislatures at all. Federal legislation by the United States may also be passed affecting these vast properties, as to which we would have nothing to say. That in itself would be a reason why the people of this country should be careful before they launch into the purchase of vast properties in a foreign country over which we have no control so far as legislation is concerned, and as to the management of, which we have nothing to say. I submit to you, Sir, that the question of owning and operating and competing as a Government with our coal mines in Nova Scotia is a particularly sore spot with the people of that province, who cannot understand how any person or any government will take the responsibility of putting themselves in competition with private enterprises. I hope that as time goes on, now that the management is under
the control of the Liberal government, the railways will show an improvement. Even in the short period towards the end of the year, the change of government has brought its results. The management knew, because they could not help reading the signs of the times, that there was to be a change of administration. Everybody believed that except perhaps the ex-Minister of Finance and his leader, and the management shaped their course to meet coming events; they were more careful, knowing that they would be submitted to the close criticism of a Liberal government and that business-like methods would be expected of them.

Perhaps it was the
anticipation of the coming government that caused the big deficit in the month of December last.

I am not aware that
there was any such deficit, but I can readily understand that the old government having gone out, if there was any possible way by which they could take anything with them they would do it. However, the inquiry that the minister has promised will see to these things, and I would advise my hon. friends opposite to be careful about anything of. that kind which they might have carried with them. I hope that as the years go on and proper management prevails in connection with these roads better results will be obtained for the good people of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
I will not undertake to make any exhaustive analysis of the statement presented by the minister to-day. It is too long and encloses within its compass so many figures, I think I might say, so much information-though I might add, were it appropriate, so little in the way of policy-that more time than a few minutes for reflection would be requisite for that purpose.
It is very rare, however, in the history of this Parliament that a minister of the Crown has presented a statement to the House which was received with a great deal more applause upon the part of the Opposition than upon the part of the Government. That has been reserved for the experience of this afternoon. I listened to the report with interest; I listened to it with some gratification, and I think the same can be said for most of the hon. members of this House. Upon the results of the operation of the national railways,

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
particularly for the year 1921, depended very much as to what would be the attitude of the people of this country toward the continuance of the system of operation then in vogue, indeed, what would be their attitude to the whole immense problem of the management of our railways.
I could not help but come to the conclusion that the Government likely thought it would be wisest that as little serious discussion should take place this afternoon on this statement as could not be avoided, and that as a consequence the Solicitor-General (Mr. McKenzie) was put up with instructions to take just as much time as he could and say as little as possible. The Solicitor-General had the accumulations of humour of all this last winter to retail to Parliament; he has had his opportunity, and that task he has mightily well performed.
The statement presented to-day of the operations in 1921 before the change of Government-and I am not for a minute suggesting that under a change of Government, if they follow the lines intimated by the minister, there will be difference in the future-is such, I am sure, that it will carry encouragement to many throughout this country, and will strengthen the hands of those who have not given up hope, who have consistently believed that we can, if we follow right lines such as have been pursued, make these roads a success.
The hon. minister's statement discloses that in the national railway management, that is to say, within the ambit of the system given to the board, the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, in all that vast system, including a mileage of 7,340 miles, there has been an improvement in operating returns in what has been the worst commercial year for many years in this country-an improvement of something over twenty million dollars. From a deficit in 1920 of 36 million odd on all those systems, there has been a reduction to about 16 millions in the year 1921. There has been at the same time, it is true, an increase in the fixed charges. Such is inevitable because the deficits that necessarily accumulated during the time of amalgamation, during the time of the rehabilitation of the road, during the time of the completion of construction and-after construction-during the time when deferred maintenance and deferred betterments had to be made up-when all these had to be overtaken, the deficits that accumulated were necessarily substantial and consequently the fixed charges increased accord-fMr. Meighen.]
ingly. The fixed charge increase this year -which if I gather the figures correctly amounts to $7,000,000, the difference between the $40,000,000 as it stands now and the 33 millions odd as it stood in 1914- will be made up in the main of the interest on last year's deficit and even in greater degree of the interest on the money put into the system in the way of betterments and in the way of increased construction, almost wholly in western Canada. But that increase is much less than the improvement that is shown in operation returns, with the consequence that a deficit of 69 millions odd announced last year is now reduced to 56 millions odd.
The minister gives us the information, which I receive with pleasure, that the deficit announced to Parliament last year of 69 millions as the 1920 deficit turns out to have been too large, and that the real deficit was $67,505,000. The difference is not great but that there is a difference on this side is something significant. It would indicate that the former Minister of Railways in giving the information last year erred on the side adverse to himself, and instead of painting the deficit as smaller than it actually was, he painted it larger. That fact surely has some significance. It stands alongside the other undoubted fact, that from the day the former Minister of Railways made it until this hour he has been condemned through the whole of the Dominion of Canada as having misrepresented the deficit, as having stated it to be far less than it actually was.
Very well, there is this improvement in the returns. It was accompanied by a small reduction of wages, but it shows itself, as disclosed in the statement of the minister as very largely due to the economies resultant upon amalgamation; to the increased traffic; to the perceptibly increased proportion of the traffic of this Dominion, indicating that the National Railway system is gaining on all competitors due to better service. The better service to the better equipment and better system brought about by the expenditures under the late administration. Anyway the corner has been turned. I want to impress again that, so far as I have discussed the subject up to now, my reference has been wholly to the roads under what we know as the National Railway Board, the board of which Mr. Hanna has been the president. That system has been in operation since, I think, the fall of 1917; I think it was put in operation just after the Union government was formed. The

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
whole mileage was not then under the board but one by one different systems have been put under it. First the Canadian Northern; and, I think at the same time, the Transcontinental railway. We did not relieve the Grand Trunk Pacific from operating that line but the Grand Trunk Pacific refused to operate it. The Grand Trunk Pacific had no more competence or power to operate it than any humble penniless individual in this House. It could not begin to operate it because of the position it was in, and absolutely declined to do so. We were powerless to make it do so because it had not the resources with which to operate the road. We had in the system then, first the Transcontinental railway and the Canadian Northern; later was added the Intercolonial. The Canadian National Railway Board was made the manager of the Intercolonial, and later in the spring of 1919 on the seventh day of May, the Grand Trunk Pacific Board having notified the Government that on that date it would cease to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific because it could not even operate that road any longer we took the Grand Trunk Pacific, operated it as receiver, and very shortly afterwards turned it over to the Canadian National lines for operation. That brought all that system under the Canadian National Railway Board. There remains now outside one only of the government-owned lines-the Grand Trunk line, the parent Grand Trunk.
Very well. In so far as this speech discloses the condition of the national railways I venture to submit to the House that it is gratifying to a degree. And more: In comparison with the record of government operation in other countries-yea, in comparison with the record of private operations during the same period in other countries-it establishes the system of management which the late government put in, as the best yet devised for the operation of government lines. For although a deficit appears, although there is a deficit on operation, although there is still a very substantial deficit in operation and fixed charges, a deficit of some 56 millions -though that is the fact, you can put the result, that is the final result, alongside of corresponding results by similar privately-owned systems in other countries, and you will find that result to reflect credit upon the operations here; a favourable result as compared with the results in the United States for the same period.
I observe that the minister has not favoured the House with any figures corresponding with those he gave us as to our own roads taken from the returns of the United States railways in the same time. In the statement given last year those figures appeared and they were illuminating indeed. Other figures appeared as to relative results over in England. They also were of very great service to Parliament. I am sorry the minister did not include these comparisons in the statement he presented this afternoon.
There is one other point I want to emphasize. In the statement made last year by the Minister of Railways estimates were given as to what would be the result for 1921. It was estimated that in 1921 there would be better results in operation, but the utmost the minister of that day expected from the year 1921 was that, in operation and in fixed charges put together we could not expect to get out under less than sixty millions odd of a deficit. The figures given this afternoon show that that has been very much reduced, at least to the extent of some $4,000,000.
Consequently, all in all, the statement this afternoon will bring to the people of Canada the realization of this truth at least-that facing, as we have had to face, the taking over a system which we had to get under and take over or let it fall into liquidation, if not into desuetude and idleness, the best course available was adopted. And, having decided on the best course, the best system of management was devised, and that system of management has been vindicated by the results.
I was not able to follow-because a parallel method was not adopted-the figures given by the Minister of Railways as regards the Grand Trunk railway. I rather came to the conclusion, from the general purport of his remarks, that the results of the 1921 operations of the Grand Trunk are by no means as satisfactory as are the results with the sister system, the Canadian National. Of course, it must be remembered that the 1921 results in the Grand Trunk are results accruing, in so far as the government board is concerned, as only from the month of May,

I will be corrected if I am wrong. I am satisfied that it was towards the end of May when what could be called a government board was put in charge of the Grand Trunk. Hon. gentlemen will remember that until that time the government was

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
not empowered to place directors in charge of the railway, the Grand Trunk directorate managed the system. The Grand Trunk Railway Company insisted, as one of the terms, which, finally, we conceded to them in making the arrangement for arbitration, that until the arbitration was over they be not ousted from control. Finally we yielded to that contention. I am not sorry that we did. If we had not yielded, there would be at least some semblance of justice in the cry that is now all too common in the Old Land that we used harsh methods in connection with the shareholders of that road. If we had ousted them, they would be able to say " Yes, you threw us out of our system, you insisted that we should get out or you would have nothing to do with us, and then, when we were out, unable to get the evidence to go before the arbitration board, you took advantage of the disability there imposed upon us, and you got the best of the arbitration." We yielded to them on that point, and as a consequence they had a right to keep their board in control of the Grand Trunk system until the time expired when the arbitration was to end. When that time expired, however, the government of the day determined, as disclosed in the speech of the former Minister of Railways, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. J. A. Stewart), that, though the arbitration was not over, it should have been over, and, as the Grand Trunk had not used due expedition to get it over, if they wanted an extension of the time they must, first of all, yield that point, and permit the government to go into control of the road. The government of the day was anxious to hasten that time when we would be able to get, to the full, the advantages of complete amalgamation of the government system. We knew we could not get them in full immediately we put our board in. We knew that some time would be required on the part of the former officers of the Grand Trunk, and on the part of some of the officers of the Canadian National railways, to prepare the way for amalgamation, to prepare the lines immediately to be pursued when the amalgamation would take effect. Consequently, we were anxious that as little delay as possible should intervene between the control of the Grand Trunk Board proper and the advent of the Grand Trunk Board appointed by the Government. The Government appointed its board about the end of May or the 1st of June last year. The 
Government retained, and necessarily retained, on the board, temporarily at least, certain high officials of the Grand Trunk. The reason for that was manifest, and the justice of it no one would dispute. The government board, therefore, only operated with part of the Grand Trunk Board, the Government appointees, from the middle of May last year until the end of the year; consequently the less favourable showing of the Grand Trunk last year, is not attributable to the fact that there was a government board in control as opposed to the old board. I do not think there are many Canadians who would not gladly agree that those gentlemen added to the board by the government were strong, able and competent men, and who would not also be glad to hear the news that men of that character, or the same men, would be accepted by this Government and continued. Very well, that was the position they were in. There has been no opportunity at all as yet to secure the fruits of that unification, which was the policy of the late government, which was embodied in and the reason of the Act of 1919. The Act of 1919 is in itself the machinery by which the whole fruits of amalgamation can be secured. It will be seen that no time whatever was lost on the part of the late administration in reaching for that goal-that goal which we must reach if our national railway management is to be a success. But, unfortunately, there has been delay on the part of this Government. I know of no reason why it should not have been called into effect immediately they came into power. What was there to ascertain? What more was there to be done? I know there was not need for further conferences between the directorates. I am aware myself, and I am sure the minister will not dispute it, that the necessary arrangements had been made, so far as the organizations of the two systems were concerned, that would have enabled the Government to have called the act into effect at once. The minister in his speech does not in any word or sentence indicate that there was any reason on that score for not calling the act into effect. He says "We had to get good men to go on the new board, and three months and a half has not been time enough to enable us to think who the good men are." Is not that the only reason the minister has given? I would venture to suggest, in the light of the results of last year as disclosed in the

C. N. R.-Minister's Statement
statement this afternoon, that the Government would do very well to reflect, in the seriousness of their own cabinet council, whether or not it is probable that there were good men on the board last year. Why, then has the Government delayed? If I have understood properly the full meaning of the statement the minister has made it is this. He says "We are going to carry out the policy of the late government; after tribulations, after doubtings, after twistings and turnings, after fears, inward quarrels, and all sorts of rebellion in the party, we have decided that we are going to pursue the very policy the late government laid down, the policy the late government pursued right up to the time it went out of power. We have decided on all that, and all we have not decided on is just when we will put it into effect." That is one statement of policy as announced by the minister this afternoon. It is not very radical or momentous, but I think on the whole it is fairly wise.
Then on the subject matter of rates, about which we have heard much for many months, I waited with apprehension-not with apprehension but with genuine curiosity-to find what the minister would have to say. I was aware, as every hon. gentleman is aware, that the control of rates on our railways was delegated, by the legislation of 1902 or 1903, to the Railway Commission of this country. I was aware that the Railway Commission was sitting and considering the problem at the present time. I was aware that the Commission had an organization that had command of the facts and the history of the whole question. I was aware that it was composed of men whom, if they were not competent men, or were in any way truant in their duty, there was a proper method of removing. I was aware the Railway Commission had been placed in this position at the hands of hon. gentlemen, many of whom are now members of the present Government; but, of course, I had to remember as well that, notwithstanding, the scale of rates in effect under that commission was laid at the door of the late government by their orators, yea, by themselves, all through this Dominion, and I was wondering what would be the policy of this administration, what line they would devise that would harmonize their own conduct in placing this question under a judicial tribunal, with their professions in declaring that they would decide it themselves. Well, we get the result this
afternoon. The whole of their policy is this: We promised in the Speech from the Throne a "consultation" of the railway heads. We have found that is no good. Here is our policy now: "We will appoint a committee of Parliament to think it over." That is the mouse that has come out of the mountain. There is going to be a committee of this House to decide what to do about railway rates. Will the Railway Commission be called as witnesses before the committee? Will we try all over again what the Railway Commission has been trying for almost a year back, or for twenty years back? If so, when is this session going to end?
I think this committee will clearly understand that the statement of the minister this afternoon disclosing the Government policy on rates is merely an admission of mental and moral bankruptcy on the whole question. There is no way in which they can carry out what they have declared they can carry out. There is no way to harmonize their professions now with their promises. There is no way in the world in which they can make good to the people of this country the promises they have made, without violating the policy of which they themselves are not only the disciples but, twenty years ago, the originators.
That is all I have to say on this question this afternoon. In so far as the facts of management are disclosed with regard to a system where the method of operation, the [DOT] personnel of operation, the system and principles of operation, have been put to the test, the statement is gratifying to me-I do not know whether it is gratifying to the Government or not. I know how far it harmonizes, or rather fails to harmonize with their statements of the position all through last fall; and as I sat here and heard those definitions of future policy-a committee of Parliament to look into the question of rates, a committee or some agent of a new board which is to be put into the National Railways to investigate whether what the National Railway Board gives out as facts are really facts or not-I wondered how far those two anaemic and equivocal definitions of policy would' be accepted by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell), as fulfilling his pledges made to the electors of his constituency during the last campaign. He was going to have a commission, a royal commission; he was going to bring over experts from Asia, no, from Europe and from some other continent which he did not name. These experts

C. N. R -Minister's Statement
were going to be brought over to Canada to supplement the brains of hon. gentlemen opposite and to study the alleged railway tangle into which the late government had plunged this country. Where is his pledge now? Can he find any reference to it in the speech of the Minister of Railways? Who is this committee or this individual whom the new board, at some unspecified time in the indefinite and misty future, is going to appoint to see whether the board itself is telling the truth or not? Is that the fulfilment of his pledge to his electors? As we received notice that the late government's plans as to amalgamation were to be followed line by line and letter by letter, I wondered what thoughts were passing through the mind of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and I wondered what comments he was making to his seat mate beside him, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), who, I see, is conferring now with his fellow pledgor, the hon. member for St. Antoine. They, speaking in Nova Scotia, and, as well, the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Putnam), used this pledge, that the Intercolonial railway was going to be jerked out of the National system when they came to Ottawa; that it was going to be extricated and restored to the Department of Railways and Canals, and run as it was in the years of long ago. I wonder now how they are going to square themselves with the electors of their constituencies. Do not let it be said that I favour the carrying out of what they were pledged to do. I favour now precisely what I said in the last campaign -precisely what the present Government is now undertaking to do at a very indefinite time, precisely what we undertook to do most definitely before the people of this country. I stated plainly in Moncton that, just as soon as we took in the Grand Trunk, as would be done at the earliest possible moment, at that time there would be sufficient eastern mileage to warrant the establishment of, and that there would be established, an Eastern Grand Division, in which there would be that measure of railway home rule that was essential, but in which there .would not be lost at all the advantages of unification. There would be, in a word such decentralisation as the Canadian Pacific has in effect, as all railways of sufficient magnitude have in effect. That was what I stated was the proper policy. That is now what is intimated in the speech of the Minister of Railways. But it is entirely out of accord with 
promises given electors, which promises account for the presence in this House of the hon. member for Cumberland, the hon. member for St. Antoine, the hon. member for Pictou, the hon. member for Colchester, and, I know not how man? more. I am not going to seek to exhaust, for it is six o'clock already, the comparison of the statement of policy on this phase this afternoon, attenuated, vague, timid, as it is, with the various bold commitments of hon. members opposite,-not at all. They were quite loose and reckless in their engagements; anything they thought would suit their constituents-that was the commitment made. One policy came from British Columbia, another policy from the prairies, another from Nova Scotia and another from New Brunswick, all designed to catch the prevailing opinion or cupidity of the district. All these policies are now scrapped, the policy which the former government sturdily pursued is now proclaimed as right and hon. members are asked by the Minister of Railways to go back and make their peace with their deluded electors.
